scenes.title: A moving interface
scenes.narration: An airway can reopen and still be injured. As an air bubble advances through liquid, it leaves a moving boundary that the epithelial cells cannot simply ignore.
scenes.credit: Conceptual drawing. Not experimental or clinical footage.
scenes.context_use: Supporting visual shown for 5 seconds of this chapter, followed by the documented/diagrammatic main picture. Does not alter narration or displace underlying original scientific evidence.

scenes.title: A controlled question
scenes.narration: The question in our experiments was physical before it was pharmacological. Could the passage of that interface damage a cultured monolayer, even without the full complexity of a lung?
scenes.credit: Published flow-chamber figure: research context only.

scenes.title: Parallel-plate flow chamber
scenes.narration: We worked with L2 alveolar epithelial cells in a parallel-plate flow chamber. The chamber let us expose cells to a controlled advancing air–liquid interface.
scenes.credit: Diagram of chamber geometry. Schematic, not measured dimensions.

scenes.title: Cells after exposure
scenes.narration: After exposure, fluorescent viability staining helped us count damaged cells. Images of the cytoskeleton gave another view of how cells responded to the mechanical event.
scenes.credit: Actual fluorescence panels not available for verification here; retained publication illustration only, not invented cell imagery.

scenes.title: What the assay sees
scenes.narration: Those colored fields were measurements, not illustrations of an entire organ. A signal could document injury without telling us, on its own, which molecular mechanism caused it.
scenes.credit: Illustrative assay logic; no invented readings.

scenes.title: Before the moving interface
scenes.narration: We also investigated whether changing the cells before exposure could alter their susceptibility. That was a test of response under specified conditions, not a claim that a treatment protects patients.
scenes.credit: Publication figure, not patient-treatment evidence.

scenes.title: The measure and its limits
scenes.narration: Making a result reproducible meant keeping the chamber, timing, controls, and image analysis intelligible. The harder part came afterward: deciding what those measurements actually allowed us to say.
scenes.credit: Explanatory geometry only.

scenes.title: An invisible injury
scenes.narration: An airway reopening looks like recovery from a distance. At cell scale, it can be another mechanical challenge. Our experiment gives that hidden event a way to be studied.
scenes.credit: Original 2021 peer-reviewed paper credited in end card.

films.title: Two Materials. No Section.

scenes.title: The angle matters
scenes.narration: Under a microscope, a zebrafish embryo can look remarkably clear. Cutting a useful series of sections is another matter. A small turn can change which anatomy a blade will reach.
scenes.credit: Actual owner-supplied specimen photograph; image does not depict histological sections.

scenes.title: The orientation problem
scenes.narration: I wanted to hold each specimen at the right angle before embedding it for histology. Two-percent agarose offered a way to keep that orientation fixed.
scenes.credit: Illustrative diagram of 2% agarose pre-embedding. Not actual footage.

scenes.title: Before the blade
scenes.narration: After processing, paraffin was supposed to support the block through the microtome. The workflow looked reasonable because each material solved a different practical problem.
scenes.credit: Photograph from the actual attempted histology preparation.

scenes.title: The section that never formed
scenes.narration: But when the blade met the block, it did not produce the ribbon I needed. Two layers separated, and fragments collected where interpretable sections should have been.
scenes.credit: Actual owner-supplied image of an unsuccessful paraffin/agarose attempt; no usable section resulted.

scenes.title: Not a machine failure
scenes.narration: The problem was not a dramatic malfunction of the microtome. What failed was the material assembly that the machine had been given to cut.
scenes.credit: Original image documents the visibly separated specimen block.

scenes.title: A question of materials
scenes.narration: Agarose is water-loving; paraffin is not. Their different behavior offers a plausible explanation for the interface, but my photographs alone cannot prove the exact failure mechanism.
scenes.credit: Material-interface explanation is a hypothesis, not an established causal analysis.

scenes.title: No corrected protocol claimed
scenes.narration: Changing the agarose grade, processing conditions, or embedding strategy might have answered it. I did not establish which correction would work, and I will not call the attempt successful.
scenes.credit: Alternatives are untested possibilities, not recommendations or successful results.
scenes.context_use: Supporting visual shown for 4 seconds of this chapter, followed by the documented/diagrammatic main picture. Does not alter narration or displace underlying original scientific evidence.

scenes.title: The experimental record
scenes.narration: I kept the photographs because they describe a real outcome: the specimen never became a usable section. An experiment can end before the measurement it was designed to produce.
scenes.credit: Original failed attempt, unaltered.

films.variant_note: Additional two-minute evidence cut. The previously published 150-second film and its captions remain available unmodified under the original filename.

films.title: The Laboratory We Carried With Us
films.topic: Chem Squad / QUACS / the scientific community

scenes.title: An organic chemistry bench
scenes.narration: In 2016, we met around an organic chemistry bench. Myrrh, nutmeg, extraction questions, and the suspicion that a traditional medicinal claim needed more than an interesting smell.
scenes.credit: Owner-supplied Chem Squad laboratory photograph; does not prove a particular extraction outcome.

scenes.title: From extract to evidence
scenes.narration: It was easy to obtain an extract and much harder to say what it contained. Identifying a constituent would still be different from proving a useful biological effect.
scenes.credit: Illustrative chemical interpretation. No drug efficacy implied.

scenes.title: Seven chemists
scenes.narration: The group that became Chem Squad included seven chemistry graduates. There was no grand institution behind us. We kept bringing papers, arguments, and new questions back to the conversation.
scenes.credit: Verified Chem Squad member photo archive; group is independent, not an institutional laboratory.

scenes.title: An ACS chapter of our own
scenes.narration: Around that period, our student chapter of the American Chemical Society at Qatar University was creating a different kind of laboratory: one open to more students and the public.
scenes.credit: Qatar University ACS chapter archive; Chem Squad and ACS are distinct initiatives.

scenes.title: Other people learning
scenes.narration: We organized demonstrations and scientific discussions. Through chapter activities, twenty-nine students had opportunities to train on instruments. The work was collective; the photographs deserve collective credit.
scenes.credit: Collective ACS activity; no photograph is attributed to a specific 29-student training session without evidence.

scenes.title: The chemistry festival
scenes.narration: Chemistry festivals taught me another form of precision: speaking clearly when the audience has every reason to question you, and resisting the urge to make a demonstration seem conclusive.
scenes.credit: Original photograph of Mahmoud hosting the fifth Chemistry Festival.

scenes.title: The conversations continue
scenes.narration: As years passed, we moved into different specialties. Some conversations continued through weekly meetings, and some through disagreements sent across a phone long after a class had ended.
scenes.credit: Member photograph is a personal archive, not footage of the weekly meetings.

scenes.title: A shared beginning
scenes.narration: There is no final group photograph that explains all of it. What the archive shows is simpler: people kept making time for scientific curiosity, even when nobody assigned it.
scenes.credit: Chemistry gathering archive; respect equal credit and distinct scientific roles.

films.title: Making Medicines Keep
films.topic: Syrups, substitution and pharmaceutical reliability in Ayyubid-Mamluk Cairo
films.status: Accepted 15 October 2026; not yet reported as formally published

scenes.title: When syrup changes
scenes.narration: A syrup can fail quietly. It can sour, crystallize, thicken too far, or disguise an inferior ingredient. In a Cairo apothecary shop, that made preparation a question of judgment.
scenes.credit: Reconstruction based on the author's historical research; not period footage or a primary source.
scenes.context_use: Supporting visual shown for 4 seconds of this chapter, followed by the documented/diagrammatic main picture. Does not alter narration or displace underlying original scientific evidence.

scenes.title: The base and the form
scenes.narration: A thirteenth-century manual, Minhāj al-dukkān, begins its syrup chapter with julāb: a base of sugar and rose water. Fruit or medicinal material gave the syrup its particular form.
scenes.credit: Original AI-assisted 2026 historical reconstruction. Not original photography, not evidence of this specific recipe or a medieval vessel. Conceptual illustration; period text attributed to al-Kūhīn al-ʿAṭṭār. Avoid invented script.
scenes.context_use: Supporting visual shown for 9 seconds of this chapter, followed by the documented/diagrammatic main picture. Does not alter narration or displace underlying original scientific evidence.

scenes.title: Qiwām
scenes.narration: The work involved heating, removing foam, straining, and recognizing when the liquid had reached qiwām: an achieved consistency. This was a practical endpoint, not a number on a laboratory instrument.
scenes.credit: Original AI-assisted 2026 reconstruction illustrating heating, skimming, and straining; not a recorded medieval experiment. Explanatory interpretation of the historical described process; not a laboratory measurement.

scenes.title: After the fire is out
scenes.narration: The manual also describes what to do when sugar crystallized or a preparation went wrong. A recipe had to account for failure after the fire was extinguished.
scenes.credit: Historical possibility illustrated without claiming that this is an authentic medieval vessel.

scenes.title: A prescription survives
scenes.narration: Another document, preserved among the Cairo Genizah papers, orders powdered ingredients to be kneaded with rose syrup. It records a therapeutic instruction, not proof that every ingredient reached the patient.
scenes.credit: Source: Cambridge Genizah Or.1081 J39. Typeset editorial depiction; original manuscript scan deliberately not reproduced without permission.

scenes.title: Substitute or adulteration?
scenes.narration: What if an ingredient was missing? The shop manual discussed substitutes under necessity, with rules tied to intended action and proportion. Replacement was not the same thing as concealed adulteration.
scenes.credit: Conceptual text diagram; historically framed substitution not modern chemical/bioequivalence.

scenes.title: Can a finished medicine be trusted?
scenes.narration: Market-oversight texts worried about false measures and deception. They also remind us of a patient’s difficult position: the finished liquid could conceal much of what happened during its preparation.
scenes.credit: Original AI-assisted 2026 reconstruction interpreting the material culture of market oversight. Not a verified historic Cairo shop. Interpretation of hisba literature; not a historical photograph or modern state regulation.
scenes.context_use: Supporting visual shown for 9 seconds of this chapter, followed by the documented/diagrammatic main picture. Does not alter narration or displace underlying original scientific evidence.

scenes.title: The article
scenes.narration: My article calls this pharmaceutical reliability, not an early version of modern manufacturing regulation. The craft, its limits, and its safeguards deserve to be understood on their own terms.
scenes.credit: Manuscript accepted by History of Pharmacy and Pharmaceuticals on 15 October 2026. Typeset bibliographic title, not a fabricated journal cover.
